title: Cqlib: A High-Performance Software Stack for Quantum Computing
authors: Tianyan Quantum Group
abstract: This paper presents Cqlib, a high-performance software stack for quantum computing built around a unified quantum circuit model. Its native Rust core provides efficient implementations of circuit processing, quantum-state and operator computation, compilation, and optimization, while Python and C interfaces support algorithm development and system integration. Cqlib covers quantum program construction, simulation, analysis, compilation, device adaptation, and result processing under consistent program semantics. Through OpenQASM and the Quantum Control Instruction Set (QCIS), Cqlib supports program representation and hardware-oriented execution. Cqlib further provides backend interfaces for device execution, with Cqlib-Tianyan serving as one implementation for QCIS-compatible quantum hardware. Evaluations using parameterized compilation tasks from Benchpress and related tests show that Cqlib achieves good functional coverage, compilation correctness, and execution efficiency within the evaluated task scope. We develop Cqlib-Algorithm as a modular library of reusable operators and composable components for widely used quantum algorithms, including quantum search, phase estimation, and variational algorithms, with additional support for error mitigation. To complement these building blocks with domain-specific workflows, we further develop Cqlib-VQE, Cqlib-QAOA, and Cqlib-QML for application-level studies in quantum chemistry, combinatorial optimization, and quantum machine learning, respectively. Cqlib also integrates source-grounded Skills and MCP-based tools to support agent-assisted program generation, backend execution, and result-guided workflow refinement. Overall, Cqlib provides a unified and extensible software foundation that connects quantum algorithm development, simulation, compilation, and execution on QCIS-compatible quantum hardware.

infographic.key_insight: Cqlib unifies quantum program development, simulation, compilation, and hardware execution around a shared circuit model and a high-performance Rust core.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Python and C interfaces, reusable algorithm modules, and QCIS-compatible backend support connect research workflows with hardware-oriented execution.
method: Use consistent circuit semantics across processing, simulation, optimization, and compilation.
Provide modular quantum algorithms and application libraries for chemistry, optimization, and machine learning.
Integrate source-grounded Skills and MCP tools for agent-assisted code generation, execution, and result-guided refinement.
infographic.evidence_signal: Benchpress parameterized compilation tasks and related tests indicate functional coverage, compilation correctness, and execution efficiency within the evaluated scope; the abstract gives no numerical results.
infographic.watch_item: Performance and portability beyond the evaluated tasks and QCIS-compatible hardware remain to be established.
infographic.paper_title: Cqlib: A High-Performance Software Stack for Quantum Computing

title: Non unitary and nonlinear quantum generative large model design and fast large-scale training without back propagation
authors: Tianze Zhu, Xiaofeng Jiang, Min Liao, Luying Zhang, Ruixi Liu, Sen Kuang
abstract: Transformer-based large models require huge computational and storage costs. Quantum computation is expected to address that due to its potential to speed up classical algorithms exponentially. Key challenges of implementing quantum large models include the linear, unitary nature of qubit evolutions contrast with the non-unitary matrices and nonlinear functions in classical Transformers, as well as the difficulty of implementing gradient back-propagation on quantum hardware. Here we propose a fully quantum large model containing all the Transformer layers, implementing the non-unitary transformations through SVD-decomposition-based quantum circuits, and approximated nonlinear activation functions through pre-trained parameterized quantum circuits. We also propose a quantum circuit training algorithm based on multi-agent Reinforcement Learning, which can train large-scale parameterized quantum circuits without back-propagation. The dependency between the inference time complexity and the model's hidden dimension has been reduced from polynomial to logarithmic, showing an exponential advantage. The inference executions on the quantum hardware verify our model's 300-1000 times speed-up, and the measurements on the sequence-to-sequence tasks shows its learning ability. The training algorithm achieves only 25% complexity of the best SOTA quantum circuit training algorithms, especially this ratio decreases fast as the parameter scale increases. Our work not only proposes a quantum large model that can significantly reduce the computational cost, but also promotes the quantum computation towards general computing.

infographic.key_insight: The paper proposes a fully quantum Transformer with non-unitary operations, approximate nonlinear activations, and training without back-propagation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The design could reduce inference scaling with hidden dimension from polynomial to logarithmic, subject to quantum implementation costs and assumptions.
method: Implement non-unitary transformations using SVD-based quantum circuits.
Approximate nonlinear activations with pre-trained parameterized quantum circuits.
Train parameterized circuits using multi-agent reinforcement learning.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports 300–1000× inference speed-ups on quantum hardware, learning on sequence-to-sequence tasks, and training complexity at 25% of leading quantum circuit training methods.
infographic.watch_item: End-to-end advantage requires scrutiny of data-loading, circuit-depth, measurement, and hardware-noise overheads not detailed in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Non unitary and nonlinear quantum generative large model design and fast large-scale training without back propagation

title: Solving the Traveling Salesman Problem Using Quantum Devices: QUBO and HOBO Formulations
authors: G. V. Shuvalov, E. N. Krivtsova, A. V. Kapranov, M. A. Remnev
abstract: The traveling salesman problem (TSP) forms the foundation for many logistics and optimization tasks. At the same time, this problem is NP-hard and requires significant computational resources. Quantum computing promises to substantially accelerate computations or increase solution accuracy. The TSP can be conveniently mapped onto the quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) formulation, which in turn can be solved using variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) and quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) methods, but this mapping requires a quadratic number of qubits. The higher-order binary optimization (HOBO) formulation requires significantly fewer qubits, but it contains higher-order terms. In our work, we thoroughly investigate both formulations and provide a practical recipe for solving the TSP. We give a comprehensive study and compare in detail QUBO and HOBO formulations.

infographic.key_insight: For quantum approaches to the traveling salesman problem, QUBO requires a quadratic number of qubits, while HOBO reduces qubit requirements at the cost of higher-order interactions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Choosing between QUBO and HOBO involves balancing available qubits against the difficulty of implementing higher-order cost terms.
method: Map the traveling salesman problem to QUBO and HOBO formulations.
Investigate variational quantum approaches, including VQE and QAOA.
Compare the formulations and provide a practical solution recipe.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a detailed comparative study but provides no numerical benchmarks, instance sizes, or measured performance gains.
infographic.watch_item: Reduced qubit requirements do not by themselves establish easier hardware implementation or quantum advantage.
infographic.paper_title: Solving the Traveling Salesman Problem Using Quantum Devices: QUBO and HOBO Formulations

title: Observable-Level Expressivity in Fixed-Readout Quantum Neural Networks
authors: Iqra Bashir, Yuanfeng Wang, Mingda Huang, Keren Li, Qi Qin
abstract: A central question in quantum machine learning is which functions of an input state a model can represent when its measurement is fixed by hardware or by experimental design. We address this question for quantum neural networks with a fixed readout observable, where the trainable pre-measurement dynamics determine the effective observable in the Heisenberg picture and the scalar output is the measured expectation value itself, without trainable affine post-processing. We characterize the reachable effective observables under three physical resource classes: unitary evolution, which preserves the spectrum of the readout; mixed-unitary evolution, which relaxes this to a majorization constraint while preserving the trace; and completely positive trace-preserving (CPTP) evolution, whose Heisenberg adjoint is unital rather than trace-preserving and therefore lifts the trace constraint inherited at the mixed-unitary level. The three reachable sets are a fixed-spectrum orbit, its convex hull, and an operator interval, and the inclusions are strict for any readout that is not proportional to the identity. The separation is witnessed locally: for a fixed Pauli readout $Z_j$ on an arbitrary number of qubits, the amplitude-damping observable $γ\id+(1-γ)Z_j$ lies outside the mixed-unitary level for every $γ>0$. We realize the CPTP level with a Stinespring-channelized circuit and derive closed-form loss floors, $4γ^2/3$ and $γ^2$ for the unitary and mixed-unitary levels and zero at the CPTP level, which the numerics reproduce within precision. Structured-observable, Rényi-moment and classification experiments illustrate how the hierarchy manifests in finite-depth ansätze. The results identify which spectral constraint each physical resource relaxes, framing reachable-observable classes as a resource for expressivity rather than an architectural advantage.

infographic.key_insight: With fixed measurement and no trainable affine output processing, reachable observables expand strictly from a fixed-spectrum unitary orbit to its mixed-unitary convex hull to a CPTP operator interval for any nonconstant readout.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Channel-based quantum circuits can represent outputs unavailable to unitary or mixed-unitary models without changing the hardware-fixed readout.
method: Characterize effective Heisenberg-picture observables under unitary, mixed-unitary, and CPTP evolution.
Use amplitude damping with a Pauli readout to witness the mixed-unitary–CPTP separation.
Implement CPTP dynamics through a Stinespring-channelized circuit and derive analytic loss floors.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerics reproduce loss floors of 4γ²/3, γ², and zero for the unitary, mixed-unitary, and CPTP levels, respectively; structured-observable, Rényi-moment, and classification experiments illustrate finite-depth behavior.
infographic.watch_item: The reachable-set hierarchy does not guarantee that a finite-depth, hardware-constrained channel implementation can efficiently reach or train toward every allowed observable.
infographic.paper_title: Observable-Level Expressivity in Fixed-Readout Quantum Neural Networks

title: Binary-Tree Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm for the Maximum $k$-Cut Problem
authors: Zhaoyang Song, Wei Zhang, Ji Cao, Xuexi Yi, Hong-Fu Wang
abstract: The maximum $k$-cut (Max-$k$-Cut) problem, as a natural generalization of the maximum-cut (MaxCut) problem, has broader applications in practical engineering. To solve this problem on quantum devices, existing studies typically encode the $k$ possible subset assignments of each vertex within the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA), which directly causes the required quantum resources to grow substantially with $k$. Here we propose a binary-tree quantum approximate optimization algorithm (BT-QAOA), which solves the Max-$k$-Cut problem by applying standard MaxCut QAOA to at most $2k-3$ subproblems. Specifically, after solving MaxCut once on the full vertex set, each subsequent step splits only the subset that yields the largest cut-value gain. This process is equivalent to constructing a binary tree whose leaf nodes after $k-1$ steps form an approximate solution to the Max-$k$-Cut problem. Furthermore, we derive a theoretical lower bound on the approximation ratio in terms of the single-step splitting quality, showing that the overall approximation ratio does not decay exponentially across multiple splits. Numerical simulations show that BT-QAOA substantially reduces the single-circuit qubit and gate overhead while maintaining a high approximation ratio, improving the estimated success probability of a single compiled circuit by orders of magnitude. This work effectively expands the practical reach of QAOA on near-term quantum hardware, offering a new route for solving more complex real-world optimization problems with limited quantum resources.

infographic.key_insight: BT-QAOA approximates Max-k-Cut through binary MaxCut splits, reducing per-circuit quantum resources without directly encoding k assignments per vertex.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could make multiway graph partitioning more practical on resource-limited quantum hardware by trading larger circuits for multiple smaller subproblem solves.
method: Run standard MaxCut QAOA on the full vertex set.
Repeatedly split the subset with the largest cut-value gain until the binary tree has k leaves.
Solve at most 2k−3 MaxCut subproblems, with a derived approximation bound tied to single-split quality.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical simulations report high approximation ratios, reduced per-circuit qubit and gate overhead, and orders-of-magnitude improvements in estimated single compiled-circuit success probability.
infographic.watch_item: Per-circuit savings do not establish lower total runtime, and the abstract reports simulations rather than hardware validation.
infographic.paper_title: Binary-Tree Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm for the Maximum $k$-Cut Problem

title: A Frequency-Learning Interpolation-Based Coordinate Descent Method to Optimize Parameterized Quantum Circuits on Quantum Hardware
authors: Jack Mandell, Adam Leicester, Zixu Wang, Jian Shi, Haimeng Zhang, Yangyang Xu
abstract: Structure-aware optimizers have been the focus of recent study for the optimization of parameters in variational quantum circuits. Many of these optimizers follow a coordinate-based paradigm, making single parameter updates by using classical approximations to the cost function generated from quantum sampling. However, the performance of structure-aware optimizers on real quantum hardware at large system size has yet to be demonstrated. Recently, Interpolation-based Coordinate Descent (ICD) has been proposed to unify many of these optimizers into one framework. ICD requires a preset frequency set for interpolation, which can be theoretically derived, but for which the cost function is generally sparse over and may require manual tuning. To address these issues, we propose Frequency-learning Interpolation-based Coordinate Descent (FLICD) to adaptively learn frequencies online, allowing easier scaling up to larger systems. We demonstrate that our algorithm is more accurate than an existing zeroth-order method COBYLA and requires fewer quantum resources than ICD on simulator. Using IBM quantum hardware, we execute FLICD on systems up to 100 qubits and observe robust performance with an increasing number of layers.

infographic.key_insight: FLICD adaptively learns cost-function frequencies during optimization, reducing reliance on preset frequency sets for parameterized quantum circuits.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Online frequency learning offers a path to scaling structure-aware circuit optimization while reducing quantum resource use relative to ICD in simulator tests.
method: Update circuit parameters using interpolation-based coordinate descent.
Learn relevant cost-function frequencies online instead of fixing them in advance.
Use learned frequencies to construct cost-function approximations for parameter updates.
infographic.evidence_signal: Simulator tests report higher accuracy than COBYLA and lower quantum resource use than ICD; IBM hardware experiments reach 100 qubits and show robust performance as circuit layers increase.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not quantify resource savings or establish whether the simulator advantages over baselines persist on noisy hardware.
infographic.paper_title: A Frequency-Learning Interpolation-Based Coordinate Descent Method to Optimize Parameterized Quantum Circuits on Quantum Hardware

title: THeatA: Transport- and Heating-aware QEC simulation with Cooling Strategies for QCCD Trapped-Ion Systems
authors: Eitaro Ishikawa, Noah Hirai, Koichiro Miyanishi, Hana Ebi, Kazufumi Tanji, Isamu Kudo
abstract: The quantum charge-coupled device (QCCD) architecture is a promising approach to scalable trapped-ion quantum computing, enabling flexible qubit interactions by transporting ions between dedicated trap zones. Programs for such systems require operations beyond conventional circuit primitives: ion shuttling, physical SWAPs, trap splitting and merging, and cooling. Motional excitation accumulated during transport increases the mean phonon number of ions and degrades the fidelity of the two-qubit Molmer-Sorensen gates. However, existing quantum error correction (QEC) simulation frameworks do not jointly track per-ion motional excitation and explicitly schedule cooling operations with their transport time and heating costs. We develop a full-stack software framework for QEC experiments and simulations on linear QCCD systems with a single ion species, comprising an intermediate representation (IR) supporting QCCD-native operations, a compiler that translates syndrome-extraction circuits into the IR, and a heating-aware noise-injection pipeline that generates noisy Stim circuits. The compiler updates the mean phonon number of each ion throughout the schedule, and the pipeline derives gate-dependent error rates from the tracked phonon states and per-ion timing, enabling the evaluation of finite-size logical-error scaling of the rotated surface code under transport- and heating-aware noise. We show that transport-induced heating prevents logical error rates from decreasing with increasing code distance under the evaluated conditions, and that indirectly cooling the ion pairs involved in two-qubit gates, by merging them with precooled coolant ions immediately before each gate, restores this decrease. By sweeping the duration and post-cooling mean phonon number of an abstract cooling instruction, we characterize their trade-off and identify the region in which logical-error scaling is maintained.

infographic.key_insight: THeatA simulations show that transport-induced heating can erase the logical-error benefits of larger QCCD surface codes, while cooling gate-ion pairs immediately before two-qubit gates can restore them.
infographic.engineering_relevance: QCCD control stacks should account for ion transport, motional heating, and cooling overhead when compiling and evaluating fault-tolerant schedules.
method: Represent QCCD-native transport, physical SWAP, splitting, merging, and cooling operations in an intermediate representation.
Compile syndrome-extraction circuits while tracking each ion’s mean phonon number and timing.
Generate noisy Stim circuits with gate-dependent errors and evaluate cooling strategies.
infographic.evidence_signal: Finite-size rotated-surface-code simulations and sweeps of cooling duration and post-cooling phonon number identify conditions where logical error decreases with increasing code distance.
infographic.watch_item: Results concern simulated linear, single-species QCCD systems and an abstract cooling instruction; hardware feasibility and cooling parameters require validation.
infographic.paper_title: THeatA: Transport- and Heating-aware QEC simulation with Cooling Strategies for QCCD Trapped-Ion Systems

title: Reducing RSA-2048 Factoring Resources Below One Billion Toffolis via LLM-Driven Verifiable Quantum Compilation
authors: Xiaodi Li, Yuqing Wang, Xue Chen, Yang-Yang Tang, Linghui Chen, Tao Zhang
abstract: Modular exponentiation dominates the logical cost of factoring 2048-bit RSA integers (RSA-2048) with Shor's algorithm. Recent approaches based on approximate residue number systems (RNS) sharply reduce the required logical qubits, yet still demand billions of Toffoli gates. Optimizing these circuits is difficult because shared ancilla qubits and measurement-based uncomputation tightly couple the arithmetic stages, while rare overflows in compressed registers occur too infrequently for random simulation to detect. Here we use large language model (LLM)-driven search to redesign the RNS pipeline across stages and build a deterministic compiler that produces a Pareto frontier of RSA-2048 circuits. We bound rare overflow probabilities analytically and verify the resulting elementary gate sequences across all constituent RNS primes on representative circuits. Relative to Gidney's 2025 baseline under matched adder accounting, our frontier cuts the minimum qubit-Toffoli product by 70.1% and lowers expected factoring Toffolis by up to 78.6% at matched accumulator precision, bringing RSA-2048 factoring below one billion Toffolis for the first time.

infographic.key_insight: LLM-driven, verifiable compilation redesigns Shor’s arithmetic pipeline to bring expected RSA-2048 factoring costs below one billion Toffoli gates.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The resulting qubit–Toffoli trade-offs could substantially reduce logical resource requirements for fault-tolerant quantum factoring.
method: Use LLM-driven search to optimize the approximate residue number system pipeline across arithmetic stages.
Generate a Pareto frontier of circuits with a deterministic compiler.
Analytically bound rare overflows and verify elementary gate sequences on representative circuits.
infographic.evidence_signal: Against Gidney’s 2025 baseline with matched adder accounting, the abstract reports a 70.1% reduction in minimum qubit–Toffoli product and up to 78.6% fewer expected factoring Toffolis at matched accumulator precision.
infographic.watch_item: These are logical circuit resource estimates; physical hardware costs and runtime remain dependent on fault-tolerant implementation choices.
infographic.paper_title: Reducing RSA-2048 Factoring Resources Below One Billion Toffolis via LLM-Driven Verifiable Quantum Compilation

title: Impact of structured noise on bosonic quantum error correction
authors: Guoyu Shu, Ling Hu, Hongbo Wu, Zhongchu Ni, Yanyan Cai, Xiaowei Deng
abstract: Bosonic quantum error correction relies on an accurate description of single-photon loss dissipation using an ideal annihilation operator, under which correctable loss errors act equivalently on different logical code states. In realistic weakly nonlinear bosonic modes, however, coupling to a structured environment can render photon loss Fock-state dependent, thereby modifying the effective dissipation operator and deforming the associated error space. Here, we experimentally investigate this effect in a three-dimensional circuit quantum electrodynamics system. By injecting spectrally engineered environmental noise into a weakly nonlinear oscillator, we observe pronounced frequency selectivity in the measured Fock-state dynamics. While the long-time transition rates converge to the Markovian limit, the transient dynamics display distinctly non-Markovian behavior, in quantitative agreement with a second-order time-convolutionless theory. By applying narrowband noise to a binomially encoded logical qubit, we further demonstrate Fock-state-dependent dissipation channels that drive logical states beyond the nominally correctable error space. These results establish structured environmental noise as a mechanism for deforming photon-loss errors in weakly nonlinear bosonic systems and highlight the need to incorporate realistic, state-dependent dissipation into the design and characterization of bosonic quantum error correction.

infographic.key_insight: Structured environmental noise makes photon loss Fock-state dependent, deforming errors beyond the space a bosonic quantum code is designed to correct.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Bosonic quantum error correction should account for environmental spectra and state-dependent dissipation rather than assume ideal photon-loss errors.
method: Inject spectrally engineered noise into a weakly nonlinear oscillator in a three-dimensional circuit-QED system.
Compare measured Fock-state dynamics with second-order time-convolutionless theory.
Apply narrowband noise to a binomially encoded logical qubit to probe error-space deformation.
infographic.evidence_signal: Measured dynamics show frequency-selective, non-Markovian transients consistent with theory, while long-time transition rates approach the Markovian limit.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not quantify the resulting logical error penalty under naturally occurring environmental noise.
infographic.paper_title: Impact of structured noise on bosonic quantum error correction

title: Quantum simulation of low-temperature impurity models
authors: Jiaqing Jiang, Nathan Ju
abstract: Quantum impurity models, which describe a small but strongly-interacting subsystem coupled to a large noninteracting bath, are the computational core of dynamical mean field theory and play an important role in simulating strongly correlated materials. We develop quantum algorithms for efficiently simulating these models at low temperatures and with high precision. For any impurity model on $n$ fermionic modes with fixed impurity size: (1) We give a quantum algorithm that prepares the thermal state at inverse temperature $β$ to precision $δ$ in time $\mathrm{poly}(n,β,\log(1/δ))$. This algorithm is the first to achieve both polynomial scaling in the inverse temperature and polylogarithmic scaling in the precision. When the Hamiltonian has an inverse-polynomial spectral gap, our quantum algorithm prepares its ground state to precision $δ$ in time $\mathrm{poly}(n,\log(1/δ))$. (2) We further give a quantum algorithm that prepares a purification of the thermal state in time $\mathrm{poly}(n,β,\log(1/δ))$. Using this purification, we estimate static and dynamical properties with error $δ$ in time polynomial in $n$ and $β$ and linear in $1/δ$ up to polylogarithmic factors, achieving the Heisenberg scaling. Our algorithms build on quantum Gibbs samplers, which are quantum analogues of Markov chain Monte Carlo methods. By using global jump operators instead of local ones, we avoid the $\exp(β)$ overhead commonly associated with quantum Gibbs samplers, making them efficient for impurity models even at low temperatures.

infographic.key_insight: For fermionic impurity models with fixed impurity size, quantum algorithms prepare low-temperature thermal states with polynomial inverse-temperature cost and polylogarithmic precision cost.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These algorithms could support quantum simulations of strongly correlated materials through impurity problems central to dynamical mean field theory.
method: Use quantum Gibbs samplers with global jump operators to avoid the usual exponential inverse-temperature overhead.
Prepare thermal states and their purifications in time poly(n, β, log(1/δ)).
Use purification to estimate static and dynamical properties with Heisenberg scaling in precision.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical complexity guarantees, including efficient ground-state preparation for inverse-polynomial spectral gaps, rather than numerical or hardware benchmarks.
infographic.watch_item: The guarantees assume fixed impurity size; practical resource costs and implementation of global jump operators remain important considerations.
infographic.paper_title: Quantum simulation of low-temperature impurity models

title: Stopping-Time Leakage in Blind Quantum Delegation
authors: Noureldin Mohamed, Saif Al-Kuwari
abstract: Blind quantum computation lets a client delegate a computation while hiding it from the server, up to a declared leakage. Its security definitions cover a single round. A variational quantum algorithm, however, delegates many rounds, and its classical optimizer decides from private data when to stop. We study what the resulting round count tells an honest-but-curious server. For protocols with one-time-padded transcripts and fresh randomness in every round, we prove that the server's best distinguishing advantage over the whole sequence equals the total-variation distance between the stopping-time distributions, so the round count is the only residual channel in this model. We also show that soundness composes as $δ\,\mathbb{E}[T]$ under adaptive stopping, given a conditional per-round soundness property that composably secure verifiable protocols provide. In simulated delegated eigensolvers for the transverse-field Ising chain, the local Polyak-Lojasiewicz ratio measured in iterations 5 to 15 predicts the noiseless stopping round with a leave-one-out error of 1.7 iterations, compared with 10.3 for a constant predictor. Across 14 configurations that differ in optimizer, stopping rule, initialization, system size, shot budget and problem family, the leakage is significant in 12 and ranges from 0.14 to 1.68 bits, and a maximum-entropy bound estimated on held-out sessions lies above it in all of them. For defense, we show that any mechanism acting after the stopping decision can only add rounds, and that differentially private padding costs the full adjacency radius. A fixed public iteration budget removes the channel completely; set at the median run length, it costs 10% of the remaining energy gap. A differentially private stopping rule based on AboveThreshold protects every pair of instances, but it must often stop too early, which makes it costly.

infographic.key_insight: Even when every delegated quantum round is blinded, the total round count can reveal private information through the optimizer’s stopping time.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Secure delegated variational quantum algorithms need stopping-time protections beyond per-round encryption, with fixed public budgets eliminating this channel at a utility cost.
method: Prove that sequence-level distinguishing advantage equals the total-variation distance between stopping-time distributions under fresh, one-time-padded rounds.
Bound adaptive-stop soundness error by δ·E[T], assuming conditional per-round soundness.
Evaluate simulated delegated eigensolvers and compare fixed-budget, padding, and private-stopping defenses.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 14 simulated configurations, leakage was significant in 12 and ranged from 0.14 to 1.68 bits; an early-iteration convergence metric predicted noiseless stopping within 1.7 iterations versus 10.3 for a constant predictor.
infographic.watch_item: The sole-channel result assumes fresh per-round randomness and one-time-padded transcripts; defenses can trade leakage reduction for extra rounds or premature stopping.
infographic.paper_title: Stopping-Time Leakage in Blind Quantum Delegation

title: Optimizing Locally Equivalent Graph States in Quantum Computing Using Greedy Best-First Search
authors: Sora Harada, Ryo Kuroiwa, Shin Nishio, Takeaki Uno
abstract: In measurement-based quantum computation and quantum repeater networks, graph-structured quantum states called graph states play a central role as an essential resource. In a graph state, each vertex corresponds to a qubit, and each edge is prepared by applying one controlled-Z (CZ) gate. Local complementation, which toggles adjacencies among the neighbors of a selected vertex, produces operationally equivalent graph states up to an inexpensive operation called local Clifford gates. Therefore, finding equivalent graphs up to local complementation with fewer edges and lower maximum degree can reduce the preparation cost, such as the number of CZ gates and the circuit depth. In this paper, we formulate the problem of finding a desirable equivalent graph via local complementations as a state space search problem. We apply a heuristic search algorithm, greedy best-first search (GBFS), to the formulated problem. Our experimental evaluation shows that despite its simplicity, GBFS outperforms existing approaches based on integer linear programming or local search across multiple graph classes, including random graphs, bounded-degree graphs, and most of the graphs constructed from quantum LDPC codes. In addition, we empirically analyze GBFS's search behavior, confirming that we need search rather than stopping at the first local minimum to find the best solution.

infographic.key_insight: Greedy best-first search finds locally equivalent graph states with fewer edges and lower maximum degree, potentially reducing quantum-state preparation costs.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Optimizing graph states can reduce CZ-gate counts and potentially circuit depth for measurement-based quantum computing and quantum repeater networks.
method: Represent graphs as search states and local complementations as transitions.
Use greedy best-first search to seek graphs with fewer edges and lower maximum degree.
Explore beyond the first local minimum to find better solutions.
infographic.evidence_signal: Experiments report improvements over integer-linear-programming and local-search approaches across random graphs, bounded-degree graphs, and most tested quantum-LDPC-derived graphs.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract provides no quantitative gains or scaling limits, and lower maximum degree does not alone establish hardware-level circuit-depth savings.
infographic.paper_title: Optimizing Locally Equivalent Graph States in Quantum Computing Using Greedy Best-First Search

title: Froq: Safe Speculative Execution on Live Quantum States for FTQC
authors: Yicheng Guang, Yueqi Chen
abstract: Reducing execution time is critical to fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) as longer executions expose logical qubits to more opportunities for failure. However, quantum processors could frequently stall due to slow classical error-correction decoders. Recent speculative decoding accelerates this process, but its speculation remains on the classical side, leaving quantum operations waiting for confirmed decoding results. Extending speculative execution to the quantum side is fundamentally challenging. Unlike classical processor states, quantum states cannot be arbitrarily copied or checkpointed for rollback, making recovery from mispredictions difficult. In this work, we propose Froq to enable safe speculative execution on live quantum states. Froq uses compiler-assisted recovery contracts to track how mispredictions propagate through quantum operations. It further employs a resource-aware runtime mechanism to reserve recovery workspace and dynamically balance the benefits of speculative execution against the expected costs of recovery. We evaluate Froq on eight FTQC programs across 88 configurations, building on an existing speculative window decoder. Froq reduces quantum-side time by 9.81% across all 88 configurations. The reduction reaches 18.34% across the 45 configurations allowing concurrent predictions, and peaks at 31.1% at code distance d=21, under limited resources.

infographic.key_insight: Froq enables safe speculative execution on live quantum states, reducing decoder-induced stalls without relying on quantum-state copying or rollback.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Compiler-guided recovery and resource-aware scheduling can shorten fault-tolerant quantum execution despite slow classical error-correction decoding.
method: Extend speculation beyond classical decoding to quantum operations.
Use compiler-assisted recovery contracts to track misprediction propagation.
Reserve recovery workspace and balance speculative gains against expected recovery costs at runtime.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across eight FTQC programs and 88 configurations, Froq reduced quantum-side time by 9.81%; reductions reached 18.34% across 45 configurations allowing concurrent predictions and peaked at 31.1% at code distance d=21 under limited resources.
infographic.watch_item: Benefits depend on available recovery workspace and prediction concurrency; the abstract does not establish performance on physical quantum hardware.
infographic.paper_title: Froq: Safe Speculative Execution on Live Quantum States for FTQC

title: Coherence transfer under bounded channel capacity
authors: Dhruv Baheti, Karol Horodecki
abstract: We investigate quantum coherence transfer between two parties whose local reference bases are misaligned, under a constraint on the capacity of the quantum communication channel. Within the resource theory of coherence, we formulate the task as maximizing the coherence received by Bob when Alice is restricted to Maximally Incoherent Operations (MIO) in her local basis. We first analyze two single-shot protocols, based on direct and locally entangled transmission, and derive their phase-optimized coherence yields. We further investigate their performance when Bob's reference basis is unknown, averaging over uniformly distributed basis configurations. In the asymptotic regime, we exploit the reversibility of coherence under MIO to characterize achievable transfer rates in terms of Alice's initial coherence. For single-qubit transmission, we derive an analytical lower bound using pure-state conversions and identify a regime in which the optimal yield saturates the channel capacity.

infographic.key_insight: Coherence transfer across misaligned local bases can be optimized under bounded quantum channel capacity, with a single-qubit regime where the optimal yield reaches that capacity.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The results provide theoretical benchmarks for transferring coherence between quantum nodes with misaligned reference bases and limited communication capacity.
method: Restrict Alice to Maximally Incoherent Operations in her local basis.
Derive phase-optimized yields for direct and locally entangled transmission, including averages over unknown Bob bases.
Use asymptotic coherence reversibility and pure-state conversions to characterize rates and bound single-qubit yields.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports analytical protocol yields, uniform-basis averages, and a single-qubit lower bound, rather than experimental hardware validation.
infographic.watch_item: Practical implementation must address whether the assumed MIO operations and basis averaging remain realistic under hardware noise and control constraints.

title: Quantum resources constrain function approximation
authors: Oxana Shaya, Lirandë Pira
abstract: Universal function approximation is central to machine learning. Quantum learning models are universal as well, but this does not specify the resources needed to approximate a given function. We study how coherence, imaginarity, entanglement and magic constrain function approximation for a fixed encoding and readout, using the cumulative resource power of the trainable gates. In a one-qubit model with phase encoding, coherence bounds the oscillation of the model function, while imaginarity bounds its odd part. In a two-qubit model, entanglement bounds the distance from product functions. These bounds hold at any encoding depth. For magic, the phase encoding itself supplies non-Clifford operations. On domains bounded away from zero, Clifford trainable gates suffice for uniform approximation. Replacing unrestricted trainable gates by Clifford gates increases the encoding depth at most polynomially in the original depth, the inverse error and the inverse distance of the domain from zero. Magic in the trainable gates can nevertheless improve accuracy at fixed depth. These results show how the resources of a quantum model must match the structure of the target function.

infographic.key_insight: Quantum resources constrain which function structures a model can approximate, while phase encoding can supply enough magic to make Clifford trainable gates sufficient on domains bounded away from zero.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Match gate resources to target-function structure, balancing approximation accuracy against encoding depth rather than relying on universality alone.
method: Analyze cumulative resource power of trainable gates for fixed encoding and readout.
Derive depth-independent bounds linking coherence to oscillation, imaginarity to odd components, and entanglement to distance from product functions.
Bound the encoding-depth overhead when replacing unrestricted trainable gates with Clifford gates.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical bounds for one- and two-qubit models and a polynomial depth-overhead guarantee, not empirical benchmarks.
infographic.watch_item: Clifford-only approximation relies on phase encoding and domains bounded away from zero; the depth overhead grows with inverse error and inverse distance from zero.
infographic.paper_title: Quantum resources constrain function approximation

title: Geometric properties of concatenated geometric and holonomic quantum gates
authors: Rasmus Wallentin, Erik Sjöqvist
abstract: We investigate the geometric properties of concatenated quantum gates, focusing on the distinction between geometric and holonomic quantum computation. We show that, although individual gates may be purely geometric, their concatenation does not generally preserve this property, since the cyclic states of the composite operation can accumulate nontrivial dynamical phases over the course of the concatenated evolution. In contrast, we demonstrate that concatenations of arbitrary single-qubit holonomic gates remain holonomic, provided that the parallel-transport condition holds throughout the evolution and the computational subspace undergoes cyclic evolution. The preservation of geometric or holonomic character under concatenation is an important prerequisite for extending arguments underlying geometric protection from individual gates to complete quantum circuits.

infographic.key_insight: Concatenating purely geometric gates need not preserve their geometric character, whereas single-qubit holonomic gates remain holonomic under parallel transport and cyclic subspace evolution.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Circuit-level claims of geometric protection require checking the full concatenated evolution rather than relying on the properties of individual gates.
method: Analyze dynamical phases accumulated by cyclic states of composite gates.
Contrast concatenation of geometric and single-qubit holonomic gates.
Establish holonomic preservation under parallel transport and cyclic computational-subspace evolution.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical results on concatenation, with no experimental data or quantitative hardware benchmarks described.
infographic.watch_item: Holonomic preservation is conditional on the stated evolution constraints and does not by itself establish hardware noise robustness.
infographic.paper_title: Geometric properties of concatenated geometric and holonomic quantum gates

title: Improved two-way capacity upper bounds for amplitude-damping channels
authors: Stefano Pirandola
abstract: We derive an improved upper bound on the two-way-assisted capacities of the qubit amplitude-damping channel with decay probability $γ$, given by $\log_2[1+(1-γ)γ^{γ/(1-γ)}]$. It applies to quantum communication, entanglement distribution, private communication, and secret-key agreement, and, for every $0<γ<1$, strictly improves the PLOB relative-entropy bound, the analytic max-relative-entropy bound, and the optimized balanced squashed-entanglement bound. At high damping, a known triple-rail protocol attains more than $99.54\%$ of its leading coefficient. Our method extends sector teleportation simulation to qubits: phase rotations and permutations give exact simulations within fixed-excitation subspaces while preserving the two-level input structure. We determine the exact, additive relative entropy of entanglement of the amplitude-damping resources and the exact regularized entanglement gain at fixed input population. We then derive explicit bounds for generalized amplitude damping, which includes thermal excitation. Combining the amplitude-damping gain with unital and entanglement-breaking channels gives a closed expression that recovers the zero-temperature result and vanishes throughout the entanglement-breaking region. It improves established benchmarks over broad parameter ranges, while the exact entanglement of the generalized resources remains open. Both results admit refinements under an average-excitation constraint. The bounds provide quantitative limits for adaptive communication through relaxing qubits and show how a sector simulation can remain useful beyond channels whose resource entanglement is known exactly.

infographic.key_insight: A new upper bound, log₂[1 + (1−γ)γ^(γ/(1−γ))], strictly tightens three established bounds on two-way-assisted amplitude-damping channel capacities for every 0<γ<1.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The bounds quantify fundamental limits on quantum communication, entanglement distribution, private communication, and secret-key agreement through relaxing qubits.
method: Extend sector teleportation simulation to qubits using phase rotations and permutations within fixed-excitation subspaces.
Determine exact additive resource entanglement and regularized entanglement gain at fixed input population.
Extend capacity bounds to thermal excitation using generalized amplitude damping.
infographic.evidence_signal: Analytical results establish strict improvements over the PLOB, analytic max-relative-entropy, and optimized balanced squashed-entanglement bounds; at high damping, a known triple-rail protocol achieves more than 99.54% of the new bound’s leading coefficient.
infographic.watch_item: The results are theoretical bounds, and the exact entanglement of generalized amplitude-damping resources remains unknown.
infographic.paper_title: Improved two-way capacity upper bounds for amplitude-damping channels

title: Direct quantum simulation of compressible Navier-Stokes flow via finite homotopy linearisation
authors: Ming-Yang Tan, Guo-Ping Guo, Zhao-Yun Chen
abstract: We develop a direct quantum simulation algorithm for finite homotopy approximations to the non-isothermal compressible Navier-Stokes equations. A primitive-variable formulation gives polynomial residuals in the fields and their spatial and time derivatives, including density-weighted time derivatives. On a periodic grid, applying each spatial stencil uniformly to every factor in a shifted product preserves the dynamics of the finite homotopy hierarchy in an affine linearisation. Because each deformation equation depends only on lower homotopy orders, the lifted generator matrix is strictly block lower-triangular and hence nilpotent. The resulting finite-polynomial solution evaluates the final state directly without time-stepping error, while explicit short-time convergence conditions bound the homotopy truncation error on a fixed grid. In two-dimensional Taylor-Green flow, initial pressure balance removes the leading longitudinal acceleration and delays the onset of dilatational kinetic energy from quadratic to quartic in time. At Mach numbers 0.2 and 0.4, the fifth-order hierarchy reproduces viscous dissipation over a longer interval than pressure-dilatation at the same relative tolerance. We identify auxiliary variables representing the same evolving product, compile the finite-polynomial evolution into logical quantum circuits, and recover a signed velocity Fourier mode via Hadamard interference. Together, the Taylor-Green energy budgets quantify the accuracy windows of each homotopy order, while coarse-grid circuits verify the signed readout and measure gate counts. For higher-order evolution on finer grids, merging coincident stencil terms and combining block-encoded products along strictly increasing homotopy-order paths substantially reduce the predicted normalisation cost.

infographic.key_insight: Finite homotopy linearisation yields a nilpotent generator whose polynomial evolution enables direct quantum simulation of approximate compressible flow without time-stepping error.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach offers a quantum-circuit route to non-isothermal compressible Navier–Stokes simulation, with energy-budget diagnostics defining observable-specific accuracy windows.
method: Form polynomial residuals in primitive variables and apply periodic-grid stencils consistently across shifted products.
Lift the finite homotopy hierarchy into a strictly block lower-triangular linear system.
Compile finite-polynomial evolution into logical quantum circuits and extract a signed velocity Fourier mode through Hadamard interference.
infographic.evidence_signal: Two-dimensional Taylor–Green tests at Mach 0.2 and 0.4 show fifth-order accuracy lasting longer for viscous dissipation than pressure-dilatation at equal relative tolerance; coarse-grid circuits verify signed readout and measure gate counts.
infographic.watch_item: Removing time-stepping error does not remove homotopy truncation or spatial discretisation error, and finer-grid circuit normalisation costs remain an implementation concern.
infographic.paper_title: Direct quantum simulation of compressible Navier-Stokes flow via finite homotopy linearisation

title: Optimal fidelity over zero-capacity erasure channels
authors: Camilo Castro-Landolt, Rabsan Galib Ahmed, Graeme Smith
abstract: Antidegradable quantum channels have zero capacity for reliable quantum communication. However, they can nevertheless transmit quantum information with nontrivial fidelity. This raises the question: how well can quantum information be preserved through such channels? In this work, we exactly characterize the optimal asymptotic entanglement fidelity of quantum erasure channels throughout the antidegradable regime. Specifically, we show that it equals $γ+\frac{1-γ}{d}$ for transmission probabilities $0<γ\le \frac{1}{2}$ and logical dimension $d$. We use fractional extendibility to establish an upper bound on the entanglement fidelity achievable by arbitrary error-correcting protocols. Furthermore, we construct a family of permutation-invariant codes that asymptotically saturates this bound.

infographic.key_insight: Zero quantum capacity does not imply zero fidelity: for erasure-channel transmission probability 0 < γ ≤ 1/2 and logical dimension d, optimal asymptotic entanglement fidelity is γ + (1 − γ)/d.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The result provides an exact fidelity benchmark for quantum error-correcting protocols operating over antidegradable erasure channels.
method: Use fractional extendibility to upper-bound entanglement fidelity for arbitrary error-correcting protocols.
Construct permutation-invariant codes that asymptotically attain the bound.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a theoretical characterization supported by a matching upper bound and asymptotically achieving code family, not experimental evaluation.
infographic.watch_item: Asymptotic attainability does not establish finite-block performance or practical encoding and decoding costs.
infographic.paper_title: Optimal fidelity over zero-capacity erasure channels

title: Differentiable collision-model control for multipartite state engineering: reachability, geometry, and preparation cost
authors: Minh Tam Nguyen, Duc-Kha Vu, Özgür E. Müstecaplıoğlu, Fatih Ozaydin
abstract: We study a differentiable control architecture for multipartite state engineering in which partial-SWAP collisions, a Heisenberg exchange, are interleaved with layers of local phase rotations. Singular collision angles confine the evolution to invariant supports, impose exact fidelity ceilings, and generate an inverse-distance lower bound on the preparation time nearby. Away from them, numerical certificates show that the sampled couplings reach the whole fixed-excitation sector for sector dimensions up to 21, and optimizations reach fidelities above 0.999 for dimensions up to 1716. At generic couplings the number of rounds needed for a given Dicke fidelity, measured by the ratio of independent phase controls to the projective dimension, is nearly independent of the system size, and the quantum Fisher information spectrum is close to that of a random Gaussian Jacobian. Near full SWAP, a slow-time theory, the sharp form of the inverse-distance bound there, predicts microscopic hitting times without fitted parameters: the distance from the singular point sets the clock and its direction selects the effective control geometry. A detuning sweep along two rays shows that the Dicke horizon follows this law up to a detuning of 0.1, where it is two to five times shorter than at a generic coupling in sectors of dimension 70 to 252, while phase-uniform, random-sign, and Haar-random targets are delayed; beyond a detuning of about 0.3 all targets return to the generic cost. The slow-time value for the Dicke target is nearly the same for sector dimensions from 35 to 252. The exchange graph of the effective theory offers an interpretation of this ordering. Counted in two-qubit gates, generic-coupling preparation is costlier than known Dicke circuits; the architecture offers fixed global couplings, local phase rotations as the only control, and no measurement.

infographic.key_insight: Near full-SWAP coupling, distance from the singular point sets the preparation clock, while detuning direction shapes control geometry and can favor Dicke-state preparation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The architecture enables multipartite state preparation using fixed global exchange couplings and local phase controls without measurement, but generic-coupling two-qubit gate costs exceed known Dicke circuits.
method: Interleave partial-SWAP collisions with local phase rotations in a differentiable control architecture.
Analyze invariant supports, fidelity ceilings, and preparation-time bounds at singular couplings.
Use numerical reachability certificates, fidelity optimization, and near-full-SWAP slow-time theory.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical certificates support full-sector reachability for sampled couplings up to dimension 21; optimizations exceed 0.999 fidelity up to dimension 1716, and near-full-SWAP Dicke preparation is 2–5× faster than at a generic coupling at detuning 0.1 in sectors of dimension 70–252.
infographic.watch_item: The near-full-SWAP speedup is target-dependent: other tested target families are delayed, and singular couplings impose exact reachability restrictions.
infographic.paper_title: Differentiable collision-model control for multipartite state engineering: reachability, geometry, and preparation cost
